name: Light Yellow
lede: Light yellow is a descriptive name for a very pale yellow, best known today as an entry in the web's X11 color list, and in older books a loose label for pale yellow pigments, dyes and fabrics.

sections.title: The web's pale yellow
sections.body: The swatch is #FFFFE0, the value of `LightYellow` in the X11 color set, which Paterson's dictionary lists under that code [1]. It is so pale that the 1955 ISCC-NBS system would call it "yellowish white", the nearest named block, at a distance of 7.6 [6]. Against a white page its contrast ratio is only 1.02, so it separates from white mostly in its warm cast [6]. An online color survey of 2010 gives a different "light yellow", the much stronger #FFFE7A, so the same two words do not fix a color [6].

sections.title: Light yellow in the old words
sections.body: Paterson gives light yellow as the gloss for many names: cowslip, [[wheat]], the obsolete *palew*, and [[buff]], which it describes as a pale yellowish brown or a light yellow [1]. [[ivory]] yellow is a light yellow approaching white [1]. The dictionary even calls the X11 color BlanchedAlmond a light yellow, though it is warmer and deeper than this swatch [1].

sections.title: Pigments and paints
sections.body:
In pigment books the phrase labels the pale end of a range. Lead chromates run from light yellow through gold to orange and red, with the lighter shades generally containing more lead sulfate [2][1]. Barium chromate is a light yellow also sold as permanent yellow or yellow ultramarine [1]. A Victorian trade writer, Salter (1869), praised a cadmium yellow as a very vivid light yellow [3], and described *di palito* as a light yellow ochre with purer tints than most ochres [4]. Thomas Bardwell's 1756 manual advises landscape greens mixed from several pigments, a light yellow ochre among them [5]. In the twentieth century the Pop painter Lichtenstein was pleased when his paint maker supplied him with several light yellows in place of one [7].

Pastoureau describes the eighteenth-century fashion for Nankin yellow, prized from the 1740s to the 1770s, which covered a range from light yellow to nearly orange and was luminous without being saturated [8].

sections.title: On the page
sections.body: A French medieval manuscript of the Lancelot-Graal, from about 1290, shows loaves of bread simply painted a light yellow [8]. The color also appears in medicine: James Hunter's 1841 table of changes in iris color lists a light yellow and a very light primrose yellow among its entries [9].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body: This color is rare in paintings. Only 28 of 23,781 archive paintings, about 0.1 percent, hold it over at least 5 percent of the canvas, and every one uses it as a highlight rather than a shadow or mid-tone [10]. The earliest is a Chinese winter scene from about 960 [10]. Seurat's *The Circus (Study)* of 1891 is one of the matches [10]. These are photographs of varnished paintings, so the colors are as photographed. In printed books, the phrase *light yellow* climbs through the nineteenth century and peaks about 1913 [10].

origin.named_after: origin undocumented; a descriptive phrase (light + yellow), fixed on the web by the X11 and CSS color lists
